# Introduction {#sec-intro}

Collections of time series can often be aggregated at several levels by geography, product, or other attributes.
Forecasts are usually needed for every series at every level, and they should be coherent: each aggregate forecast should equal the sum of the forecasts below it.
Forecast reconciliation achieves this by forecasting every series independently and then adjusting the forecasts to satisfy the aggregation constraints [@hyndman2011optimal; @athanasopoulos2023forecast].
The minimum trace (MinT) method of @wickramasuriya2019optimal chooses the adjustment using the covariance matrix of the base forecast errors, and it is now the standard approach.

Reconciliation is almost always applied to one variable at a time, yet many hierarchies carry several variables.
A retailer, for example, may need forecasts of both unit sales and revenue for every store, with each variable summing across stores to regional and national totals.
The two variables are measured in different units, but both respond to the same promotions, holidays and local demand, so their forecast errors are correlated.
Because MinT works by exploiting the covariance of the base forecast errors, it seems natural to reconcile both variables together, using a covariance matrix that spans them, and to expect this to beat reconciling each separately.
We ask when joint reconciliation is better than reconciling each variable separately.

Joint reconciliation of several variables is not the same problem as reconciling a grouped hierarchy.
In a grouped hierarchy, such as sales disaggregated by both region and product type, the categories of each grouping variable are linked by aggregation constraints: total sales is the sum over products or over regions, and that total is itself forecast.
Here unit sales are never added to revenue.
The stacked summing matrix is block diagonal by variable, and the only link between the variables is the error covariance.

Some cross-variable dependence is already known to be of no use to reconciliation.
MinT is unaffected by any component of the error covariance that lies in the coherent subspace [@wickramasuriya2021properties], so cross-variable dependence of that form is invisible.
When the error covariance is separable (i.e., a Kronecker product of a cross-variable matrix and a cross-series matrix), joint and separate reconciliation coincide whatever the cross-variable correlation.
This follows from a result of @girolimetto2025cross for cross-temporal reconciliation, and it is the reconciliation analogue of Zellner's observation [@zellner1962efficient] that seemingly unrelated regressions with identical regressors reduce to equation-by-equation least squares.
These conditions are sufficient, but they do not say which forms of dependence joint reconciliation can exploit, or by how much.

Our approach is to write MinT as a regression of the base forecast errors on the observed incoherences of the base forecasts.
In this form, the question becomes whether one variable's incoherences carry information about another variable's errors beyond what that variable's own incoherences provide.
This leads to a necessary and sufficient condition for joint and separate reconciliation to coincide, which includes the known cases above.

In practice, we need to know whether this condition holds for a given data set, and if not, how much the departure affects the forecasts.
We propose two effect sizes: $\kappa$, the weight that the joint reconciliation places on other variables' incoherences, and $\gamma$, the reduction in mean squared error that it would deliver if the estimated covariance were correct.
We also propose a likelihood ratio test of the condition, which uses the regression form of MinT and needs no simulation.

We study the effect of joint reconciliation in two simulation experiments, one in which the error covariance is controlled directly and one in which base forecasting models are fitted to simulated series.
We also explore joint reconciliation in an application to monthly worker admissions and dismissals in Brazil's 27 federative units, which aggregate to five regions and to the country.
Besides the forecasts of each variable, we consider quantities that combine the variables.
Net employment change, the difference between admissions and dismissals, is the headline figure in Brazil's official monthly employment statistics.
Its forecast distribution depends on the joint distribution of the base forecasts, so for probabilistic forecasts we ask whether the dependence between the variables should be modelled when the base forecasts are simulated, when they are reconciled, or both.

@sec-setup sets out notation and the reconciliation problem for several variables.
@sec-theory gives necessary and sufficient conditions for joint and separate reconciliation to coincide, and their consequences.
@sec-diagnostic develops the effect sizes and the test.
@sec-simulation reports the two experiments, @sec-application the application to Brazilian employment, and @sec-discussion discusses the implications.
